items.title: What we know so far after Krakow gun attack
items.tldr: A 25‑year‑old Polish man opened fire in Krakow’s Main Market Square, killing six people and wounding sixteen. The attacker, suspected of far‑right ties, was shot by armed officers and later arrested, prompting a nationwide mourning period and renewed debate over extremist radicalisation.
items.background: Krakow, Poland’s second‑largest city, sits at the crossroads of Central Europe’s cultural heritage and a modern urban environment. Recent years have seen a rise in far‑right activity across the Visegrad region, with incidents in Hungary, Slovakia and Poland reflecting a broader trend of ideologically motivated violence. This attack underscores how lone‑wolf perpetrators, often inspired by online radicalisation, can strike in densely populated public spaces, challenging traditional counterterrorism frameworks that have historically focused on organised groups.

analysis.heading: Immediate Tactical Response and Law Enforcement
analysis.content: The police response was rapid and coordinated. Armed officers engaged the shooter within three minutes of the first shots, using lethal force that stopped further casualties. Body‑cam footage captured the confrontation, showing the officer confronting the suspect before being injured. The swift intervention highlights the effectiveness of Poland’s police tactical units, yet also raises questions about the preparedness of first responders in similar open‑air, high‑visibility locations across the EU.

analysis.heading: Political and Geopolitical Ramifications
analysis.content: Prime Minister Donald Tusk framed the incident as a "drastic case of terrorism," marking a shift in Polish discourse toward recognising domestic far‑right extremism as a security threat comparable to international jihadist plots. The EU’s top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, described the shooting as a tragedy with implications beyond Poland, hinting at possible coordination on extremist monitoring across member states. The attack also reignited debates over firearm licensing in Poland, where the suspect legally owned a weapon, prompting calls for stricter background checks and potential re‑classification of certain far‑right propaganda as incitement.

analysis.heading: Societal Impact and Counter‑Extremism Measures
analysis.content: The massacre shocked both locals and tourists, many of whom witnessed the chaos firsthand. Social media platforms saw a surge in posts discussing far‑right ideologies, prompting calls for platform accountability. In response, the Polish Interior Ministry announced a review of existing counter‑terrorism strategies, including enhanced surveillance of extremist online forums and increased funding for de‑radicalisation programmes. The tragedy also spurred civil‑society groups to push for greater mental‑health resources and community‑level resilience building, recognising that early intervention can mitigate the risk of lone‑actor attacks.

key_facts: Six people were killed (four women, two men), including a British national; three bodies were later discovered at the attacker’s home.
The gunman, a 25‑year‑old Polish male, was identified but not publicly named; he was armed with a military‑grade rifle and had a firearms permit.
Sixteen individuals were hospitalised, among them two police officers who were shot while detaining the suspect.
The suspect’s vehicle contained multiple weapons and ammunition; no explosives were found.
Krakow’s mayor declared a mourning period until 11 November, and the Polish government ordered a full investigation supported by counter‑terrorism police.
implications: The attack may prompt EU‑wide policy revisions on gun control, especially regarding permits for individuals with extremist affiliations.
It highlights the need for improved intelligence sharing between national law‑enforcement agencies and tech platforms to detect early signs of radicalisation.
items.outlook: In the coming weeks, Poland is expected to release a comprehensive report on the attacker’s online footprint, leading to potential legislative reforms and a renewed focus on deradicalisation programmes. International partners, including the United States and the European Commission, have offered assistance in investigative techniques and threat analysis, suggesting a collaborative approach to combat the rising threat of far‑right lone‑wolf violence across Europe.

items.fulltext:
What we know so far after Krakow gun attack
- Published
At least six people were killed and several others injured when a gunman suspected to have ties to the far-right opened fire in central Krakow, the second largest city in Poland.
Three bodies were found at his home when it was searched by police. Here's everything we know so far.
How did the attack unfold?
The attack began shortly before 15:00 local time (14:00 GMT) in Krakow's Main Market Square, the bustling central point of the city.
Police said a man drove into the square before beginning to fire "at random people from his car".
Footage from the scene shows scenes of panic as people fled, with the sound of gunfire clearly heard.
A passing tram was shot at during the apparently random attack, shattering windows but no passengers were injured.
Armed officers raced to the scene and engaged in a gunfight with the attacker, who was shot within three minutes of the attack beginning, preventing a further massacre, officials said.
The gunman was shot but is alive and has been arrested.
Distressing footage authenticated by BBC Verify shows the moment a police officer confronts the suspect on the ground before firing his weapon several times.
The officer then falls to the ground, apparently having been injured himself.
Shop windows in the square have signs of damage, seemingly from bullets, with glass shards scattered along the floor.
City officials have urged people who live in the city and tourists to stay away from the area while an investigation continues.
The suspect's car, found at the intersection of Dietla and Stradomska streets, was checked for possible explosive devices, police said, but none were found. Residents of nearby buildings had been evacuated while the operation was under way.
How many people have died and been injured?
Six people - four women and two men - are confirmed to have been killed, including a British national. Three victims are Polish and two have not been identified.
Sixteen people, including five foreigners and the attacker, were taken to hospital. Among those being treated are two police officers who were shot while detaining the attacker. The interior ministry later said they were from Britain, Austria, Russia, Germany and Portugal.
Poland's Prime Minister Donald Tusk later named the injured officers as Senior Constable Jakub Kulik and Senior Constable Artur MoraÅski.
Tusk said three bodies - two women and one man - were found at the gunman's house when it was searched after the attack.
One of the police officers was described as being in a "very critical condition" by a Polish government minister after being shot three times while arresting the attacker. The officer is undergoing surgery, he added.
Polish authorities have not confirmed the names and ages of the other victims.
What do we know about the suspect and motive?
Police have identified the attacker as a 25-year-old Polish man but have not confirmed his name.
The suspect was wearing "military-style attire" and had a military-grade weapon, according to a police spokesperson. However, authorities have confirmed the attacker was not a soldier.
"Many pieces of weapons and ammunition were found in his vehicle", the spokesperson added.
Polish media has reported the suspect had a firearms permit and may have obtained the weapons from his family home.
A minister has said early investigations indicate he was inspired by "far-right ideologies". The minister also described him as an "ultra-nationalist" without giving further details.
His home is being searched with support from counter-terrorism police.
How did witnesses describe the attack?
The shooting happened in one of the largest medieval squares in Europe, a busy location which is also a popular tourist destination.
Jonathan Balshaw from Ipswich was there with his Polish girlfriend Dominika. The couple were outside St Mary's Basilica, in the corner of the square, when the shooting started.
Jonathan said: "We ran down the side of the church and through the side door and hid with several other people until the gunfire died down.
"A lot of shots were fired, more than 20 with it sounding like multiple different firearms - there were two distinctly different noises."
Caitlin Shasby from Newcastle arrived in Krakow yesterday with her friend Jon for a long weekend.
She said they heard shots from their hotel room but were not sure what was happening until their hotel rang them and told them to "stay in our rooms until further notice".
What has the reaction been in Poland and internationally?
After travelling to Krakow, Prime Minister Donald Tusk said : "Until now in Poland we haven't had such drastic cases of terrorism...that's what we have to call this cruel attack on people's lives here in Krakow."
Krakow Mayor Åukasz GibaÅa has signed an order declaring a period of mourning in the city which will last until Wednesday, 11 November.
US ambassador to Poland Tom Rose described it as a "savage and murderous attack".
The EU's top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, said the shooting was "a tragedy that will be felt far beyond Poland".

items.title: No clear winner after tight New Zealand general election
items.tldr: Preliminary results from New Zealand's 2026 general election show a hung parliament with the centre‑right National Party winning 42 seats, 19 short of a majority. Labour secured 36 seats, and smaller parties – Greens, ACT, New Zealand First, the new Opportunity Party and Te Pāti Māori – hold the balance of power, setting the stage for weeks of coalition negotiations.
items.background: New Zealand uses a mixed‑member proportional (MMP) system that almost always produces coalition governments. The 2026 campaign was dominated by cost‑of‑living pressures, rising unemployment and a record outflow of citizens to Australia. With more than 99 % of votes counted, the two major parties together captured only about 60 % of the party vote – a historic low – reflecting growing voter fragmentation and the entry of the centrist Opportunity Party, which crossed the 5 % threshold for the first time.

analysis.heading: Fragmented mandate and the role of minor parties
analysis.content: The combined seat count of National (42) and its traditional partners ACT (13) and New Zealand First (12) yields 67 seats, still short of the 61‑seat majority needed in the 120‑seat House. Labour (36) plus the Greens (16) and Te Pāti Māori (5) also fall short at 57. The decisive bloc is the Opportunity Party (7 seats), which has declared willingness to negotiate with either side. Professor Andrew Geddis notes that the party’s ‘wildcard’ status means the final government could hinge on a few thousand special votes still to be counted, especially in marginal electorates.

analysis.heading: Economic discontent driving voter volatility
analysis.content: Polling by Roy Morgan shows cost of living as the top issue for a majority of voters. Julian McCrann highlights that Prime Minister Christopher Luxon’s 2023 promise to improve living standards has not materialised, with more than half of New Zealanders now saying the country is no longer a ‘land of opportunity’. Record net migration to Australia underscores the depth of economic anxiety, feeding support for newer parties that pitch generational renewal and pragmatic policy over ideological loyalty.

analysis.heading: Coalition dynamics under MMP
analysis.content: MMP incentivises post‑election bargaining rather than pre‑election alliances. Both Luxon and Hipkins have signalled a caretaker government while special votes are processed (due 27 November). The Greens’ proposal to force supermarket divestments into public ownership adds a policy flashpoint that could either attract or repel potential partners. The need for compromise across a broad ideological spectrum – from free‑market ACT to Māori‑focused Te Pāti Māori – suggests any coalition agreement will be fragile and policy‑heavy.

analysis.heading: Implications for New Zealand’s international posture
analysis.content: A prolonged formation period may delay foreign‑policy decisions, notably on trade negotiations with the Indo‑Pacific Economic Framework and climate commitments at COP30. However, the presence of the Opportunity Party, which advocates a ‘future‑focused’ agenda, could push any government toward a more multilateral, technology‑oriented stance, aligning with broader Western efforts to diversify supply chains away from China.

key_facts: National Party 42 seats; Labour 36 seats; Greens 16; ACT 13; New Zealand First 12; Opportunity Party 7; Te Pāti Māori 5.
Combined major‑party vote share ~60 %, a historic low under MMP.
Opportunity Party crossed the 5 % threshold for the first time and is open to either bloc.
Special votes (including overseas) remain uncounted; official result due 27 November.
Cost of living and unemployment were the dominant campaign issues.
implications: Extended coalition talks could create a policy vacuum lasting several weeks.
Minor parties gain disproportionate leverage, potentially reshaping economic and social policy.
Voter fragmentation signals a long‑term shift away from two‑party dominance in New Zealand politics.
Uncertainty may affect investor confidence and delay trade‑policy initiatives.
items.outlook: The next three weeks will be decisive as special votes are tallied and party leaders enter formal negotiations. The most probable outcome is a centre‑right coalition anchored by National, ACT and New Zealand First, with the Opportunity Party providing confidence‑and‑supply or a formal partnership. However, a centre‑left arrangement led by Labour, the Greens and Te Pāti Māori, also backed by Opportunity, cannot be ruled out. Either scenario will produce a government reliant on cross‑party compromise, making policy implementation slower but potentially more durable.

items.fulltext:
No clear winner after tight New Zealand general election
- Published
There was no clear winner following New Zealand's election on Saturday, as the leaders of its two major parties preparing for negotiations to form a coalition government.
Prime Minister Christopher Luxon's centre-right National Party won 42 seats but was 19 short of the simple majority needed to form a government, despite being the largest party, preliminary results show.
Combined with their coalition partners ACT and New Zealand First, they would have a slim lead over the left-leaning bloc if a deal could be reached.
But opposition leader Chris Hipkins, whose Labour Party won 36 seats, showed no signs of conceding, saying the "shape of the next government" will remain uncertain "for a while".
The tight result followed a campaign shaped by the cost of living and unemployment.
Projections show the National Party on 42 seats and Labour on 36. The Greens are on 16, with ACT on 13, New Zealand First on 12, the Opportunity Party on 7 and Te PÄti MÄori, which represents MÄori interests, on 5.
The electoral commission was not due to announce the official result until 27 November.
Luxon congratulated Hipkins on a "very hard-fought race" before addressing party colleagues, saying "whatever the final count, we are incredibly proud of each and everyone for you".
He said he would run a caretaker government until the final results were confirmed later in the month, adding: "With those final results there can then be meaningful negotiations."
Elsewhere, Labour leader Hipkins said "the people have spoken", adding: "It may take a bit longer to work out what they've said."
Hipkins said the results made clear the "next parliament is going to require all of us to compromise, to work together and to find a common ground".
More than 99% of votes have been counted in New Zealand, with National and Labour neck-and-neck in terms of vote share.
But the preliminary results pointed to historically low support for the two major parties, with a combined vote share of around 60%.
They were followed by the Greens, ACT, New Zealand First, centrist party Opportunity and Te PÄti MÄori, which represents MÄori interests.
- New Zealand election 2026: What you need to know 
  - Published27 October
The Opportunity Party crossed the 5% threshold to enter parliament for the first time, with leader Qiulae Wong saying would work with either side.
It has been described as this election's kingmaker as it remains open to working with either major bloc, but its leaders said they would negotiate first with the party that secures the most seats.
Speaking at Opportunity's watch party, Wong told supporters: "We believe that we can change the way we do politics to focus on the future, on the next generation, and on finding common ground."
Professor Andrew Geddis from the University of Otago, an expert in election law, said "the Opportunity Party as a wildcard player" could "determine which bloc of parties is able to govern".
"It will come down to some very fine vote margins not just between the parties, but in individual electorates. We are going to have to wait for the special votes to be processed and counted over the next three weeks," he said.
Special votes are votes cast outside a voter's electorate, including overseas.
The Greens â who have proposed forcing the country's two main supermarkets to divest stores to create publicly-owned shops â saw their vote rise by a couple of percentage points.
Julian McCrann, head of polling at Roy Morgan, told BBC News the cost of living was the main issue for many New Zealanders
"Three years ago, Luxon came in saying he'd be making New Zealanders' lives better and solving these economic issues, but he hasn't really delivered," he said.
More than half of the country no longer see New Zealand as a land of opportunity, according to an annual social cohesion survey. Record numbers of Kiwis have been leaving the country, with many going to Australia.
New Zealand's mixed-member proportional voting system means most governments are coalitions.
Each voter makes two choices â for the representative of their constituency in parliament and a political party.

items.title: Parliament restoration delays 'frustrating', says Commons Speaker
items.tldr: Sir Lindsay Hoyle has voiced frustration over the stalled £40 bn Palace of Westminster restoration, warning the project could span six decades and leave the historic building exposed to fire. The public accounts committee labels the situation a “crunch time”, highlighting £420 m of taxpayer loss per year of delay and incomplete safety upgrades. Political and legislative hurdles are now the primary obstacles to securing the necessary funding and commencing essential repairs.
items.background: The Palace of Westminster restoration programme, launched in the early 2000s, was intended to address severe structural decay, fire‑safety deficiencies, and pervasive asbestos contamination. Early reports a decade ago warned of an “impending crisis” due to outdated wiring, Victorian‑era piping, and inadequate fire‑suppression systems. Since then, successive governments have struggled to secure the £40 bn needed, and a series of legislative requirements have forced Parliament to approve the entire scope and financing before any work can begin. The current process has turned the project into a case study of how bureaucratic inertia can exacerbate a national heritage emergency.

analysis.heading: Financial Escalation and Taxpayer Burden
analysis.content: The financial implications of the delay are staggering. The public accounts committee estimates that each additional year without progress costs the exchequer £420 m, effectively inflating the total price tag beyond the original £40 bn estimate. With the timeline now projected to 61 years, the cumulative taxpayer exposure could exceed £100 bn if the current pace continues. This escalating cost not only strains public finances but also fuels political resentment, as voters question why essential heritage and safety works are being deferred. The committee’s warning that the building could be left vulnerable to a Notre Dame‑style catastrophe underscores the urgency of breaking the fiscal deadlock.

analysis.heading: Safety Vulnerabilities and Asbestos Crisis
analysis.content: Fire‑safety and asbestos concerns remain the most immediate threats to occupants and the public. Despite years of advocacy by the Speaker, a fire‑suppressing mist system has yet to be installed across the historic chambers, leaving the most vulnerable areas—such as the Central Lobby and the historic chambers—without modern protection. Simultaneously, repeated asbestos discoveries have forced periodic evacuations and halted work in sections of the building. The combination of outdated electrical networks dating back to the 1940s, Victorian plumbing, and the lack of a comprehensive fire‑suppression network creates a perfect storm for a disaster that could jeopardize parliamentary continuity and national heritage.

analysis.heading: Legislative Gridlock and Political Obstacles
analysis.content: The core legislative hurdle is the requirement under the Parliamentary Buildings Act that the entire project scope and funding must be approved by Parliament before any works can commence. This “all‑or‑nothing” clause has effectively frozen the programme, as competing political priorities and funding negotiations stall consensus. Recent discussions among government whips suggest a possible debate and vote before the end of 2026, but no concrete date has been set. The Speaker’s call for incremental works—renovating problem areas rather than waiting for a full‑scale overhaul—clashes with the current legal framework, highlighting a need for legislative reform to allow phased interventions while preserving accountability.

key_facts: Total projected restoration cost: up to £40 bn.
Estimated timeline: 61 years.
Annual cost of delay to taxpayers: £420 m.
Fire‑suppressing mist system not yet installed.
Multiple asbestos discoveries have halted work in several areas.
Public accounts committee labels the situation a “crunch time”.
Legislative requirement mandates full project approval before any work begins.
implications: Continued fiscal drain on public finances, potentially exceeding £100 bn.
Elevated risk of a catastrophic fire that could destroy a key national landmark.
Erosion of public confidence in the government’s ability to manage large‑scale heritage projects.
Potential need for alternative financing models, such as public‑private partnerships or ring‑fenced bonds.
Pressure on Parliament to reform the Buildings Act to allow phased, safety‑critical works.
items.outlook: If the legislative impasse is not resolved, the restoration programme will remain mired in delay, compounding both financial and safety risks. The most plausible near‑term scenario is a parliamentary vote on a limited £3 bn initial works package by early 2027, allowing critical fire‑safety upgrades and asbestos removal to proceed while the broader financing debate continues. However, without a clear long‑term funding strategy, the Palace of Westminster will continue to teeter on the brink of a heritage emergency, threatening both its historic integrity and the continuity of UK democratic functions.

Parliament restoration delays 'frustrating', says Commons Speaker
- Published
The Speaker of the House of Commons has expressed "frustration" with the lack of progress on restoration to protect the Palace of Westminster.
Sir Lindsay Hoyle told the BBC the current process for approving essential renovations to Parliament amounted to "putting ourselves in handcuffs", and said more time was spent "doing surveys" than getting repairs under way.
The Commons public accounts committee this week warned it was "crunch time" for the ailing building's restoration, which could cost up to Â£40bn and take 61 years.
It said every additional year of delay cost taxpayers Â£420m, while its chairman warned the Palace could be left vulnerable to a devastating fire like that which engulfed the Notre Dame.
Sir Lindsay said his "biggest frustration" with the Victorian building's restoration was that "we're not getting on with the work".
"We spend more time doing surveys," he told BBC Radio 4's The Week in Westminster. "Instead of doing surveys, why don't we start repairing the building?"
The Speaker criticised current legislation which means the main renovations cannot begin until Parliament has approved the entire project's scope and funding.
"It's very frustrating when the Act of Parliament prevents you carrying out the major repairs that you need to. Talk about putting ourselves in handcuffs."
He added: "What we have to do is renovate and repair the problems areas."
- More asbestos found in Parliament, as MPs urged to get on with revamp 
  - Published2 days ago
- Parliament revamp could cost Â£40bn and take 61 years 
  - Published5 February
Sir Lindsay also questioned why a fire-suppressing mist system had not yet been introduced throughout the building, even though he has called for it for years.
"The major part and the most historic parts of the building haven't got it, and that's what we need."
Asked about reports that Parliament might be given an opportunity to vote on the way forward before the end of 2026, Sir Lindsay said that was a matter for government business managers.
"Who knows when it's going to come forward? Let's see what the House decides," he said.
Much of the 19th-Century building's network of wires and pipes dates back to the 1940s - and some to the Victorian era - according to a report, external which warned of an "impending crisis" a decade ago. Fire safety issues and high levels of asbestos have also been identified.
The BBC understands government whips have discussed holding a debate and vote by the new year, but no date has been scheduled.
This would decide whether to proceed with up to Â£3bn of initial works and narrow down four current options, ahead of a final decision by 2030.
One proposed option would see MPs and peers move out of the site for up to 24 years from 2032, costing up to Â£15.6bn.
Another involves moving only the House of Lords out of the building, costing Â£39bn and taking 61 years.
The chairman of the body in charge of refurbishing Parliament defended the potential costs earlier this year, telling the BBC: "We're already spending Â£150m a year trying to keep the thing standing."

items.title: PM tells firms to publish salaries in job adverts ahead of new law
items.tldr: Prime Minister Andy Burnham urges businesses to voluntarily disclose pay details in job ads, ahead of upcoming legislation aimed at increasing transparency, preventing discrimination, and narrowing the gender pay gap.
items.background: The United Kingdom is on the cusp of a landmark employment‑rights reform. While the European Union already mandates that employers list initial pay or a salary range in job postings, the UK has so far relied on voluntary practice. A recent consultation by the Cabinet Office, which closed in summer 2026, recorded an overwhelming 94 % of respondents backing greater pay transparency. The push comes amid growing concern over the nearly one‑million young people classified as NEET (not in education, employment or training) and a broader effort to curb systemic pay discrimination, especially gender‑based gaps. The government’s latest move—urging firms to publish salaries now, before a compulsory law is enacted—reflects a strategic blend of moral suasion and regulatory preparation.

analysis.heading: Policy Rationale and Public Support
analysis.content: The government frames salary disclosure as a consumer‑rights issue for job seekers. By making pay information visible, applicants—particularly first‑time workers—can make informed decisions, reducing the “soul‑destroying" uncertainty of applying to anonymous listings. The policy also targets structural inequities: transparent adverts are seen as a lever to expose unjustified pay gaps, empower workers to challenge discrimination, and help close the gender pay divide. The Cabinet Office’s consultation results—94 % in favour—demonstrate strong public appetite, suggesting that the measure enjoys cross‑party resonance and is unlikely to face significant grassroots opposition. Moreover, the timing aligns with the Milburn Review’s forthcoming report on youth inactivity, indicating that pay transparency is being positioned as a tool to re‑engage NEETs in the labour market.

analysis.heading: Industry and Political Repercussions
analysis.content: While the principle of openness garners broad support, practical implementation raises concerns. The Confederation of British Industry and the CIPD caution that pay determination is a nuanced process, often dependent on a candidate’s skills, experience, and potential. They argue that a one‑size‑fits‑all regulatory approach could stifle flexible remuneration structures, especially in sectors where performance‑based pay is critical. Politically, the Labour government faces pushback from the Conservative shadow business secretary, Julia Lopez, who contends that businesses should retain discretion over what information they disclose, provided they act honestly. The opposition’s stance highlights a potential partisan split, with Labour framing transparency as a social‑justice imperative and the Tories emphasizing market autonomy. Additionally, some MPs are themselves advertising roles without salary details, prompting questions about consistency and fairness within the legislature.

analysis.heading: International Alignment and Future Outlook
analysis.content: The UK’s proposed rules mirror emerging EU directives that require employers to list initial pay or a range in job adverts, either within the posting or before an interview. This convergence suggests a broader Western‑hemisphere trend toward labour‑market transparency, driven by digital platforms that can easily embed salary data. Looking ahead, the government has signalled that further details on enforcement mechanisms and the precise scope of required information will be released “in due course.” If the voluntary phase yields high compliance, the legislative rollout could be smoother; however, a backlash from sectors that rely on opaque compensation could force the government to adopt a phased or sector‑specific approach. The outcome will likely influence not only UK employment practices but also how other jurisdictions balance market flexibility with equity in pay disclosure.

key_facts: Prime Minister Andy Burnham has called on firms to publish salaries in job adverts voluntarily, ahead of a forthcoming law that will make such disclosure mandatory.
A Cabinet Office consultation in summer 2026 recorded 94 % support for greater pay transparency.
The government aims to reduce the nearly one‑million NEET young people and curb pay discrimination, especially the gender pay gap.
EU member states already require employers to disclose initial pay or a salary range in job postings.
Industry bodies such as the CIPD note that pay setting is complex and that broad regulation may be unsuitable for all sectors.
Conservative shadow business secretary Julia Lopez criticised the move, arguing that businesses should decide what information to publish.
The Equality and Human Rights Commission described publishing salaries in adverts as a “positive step” and called for additional measures, such as responding to pay‑related questionnaires.
implications: Increased applicant pool and better job‑fit for employers who disclose salaries, as noted by Adzuna co‑founder Andrew Hunter.
Potential reduction in gender pay disparities as pay gaps become more visible and challengeable.
Higher compliance costs for firms that need to redesign job adverts and possibly adjust remuneration policies.
Political pressure on MPs and public sector bodies to adopt the same transparency standards they advocate for private firms.
Possible ripple effects on UK‑EU trade negotiations if divergent pay‑disclosure standards emerge.
items.outlook: The UK’s push for mandatory salary disclosure marks a decisive shift toward a more transparent labour market, aligning domestic policy with EU best practice and responding to public demand for fairness. If the voluntary phase achieves near‑universal compliance, the legislative phase should proceed smoothly, cementing the UK’s reputation as a leader in pay‑equity reform. Conversely, significant industry resistance or political deadlock could dilute the reforms, leaving the gender pay gap and NEET challenges only partially addressed. Stakeholders—employers, trade unions, and civil‑society watchdogs—will need to collaborate to balance operational flexibility with the societal benefits of openness, ensuring that the new rules deliver tangible improvements in job quality and workplace equity.

items.fulltext:
PM tells firms to publish salaries in job adverts ahead of new law
- Published
Businesses should publish salaries in job adverts now, Prime Minister Andy Burnham is telling firms, rather than wait for a new law to come in that will force them to do so.
The government is planning to make pay details compulsory in adverts, with legislation on the issue being brought forward "as soon as possible".
It argues the change will help jobseekers, particularly those applying for their first job, and could help prevent pay discrimination. However, one industry group said setting pay was a complex process and regulating adverts was not always suitable.
It comes a week after the UK's equality watchdog said employees should legally be able to find out what their colleagues are earning.
Burnham said the current system felt "weighted against the applicant" and the changes were aimed at "tilting the scales back".
"It can be quite soul destroying for young people these days, applying for jobs when the salary is not listed but sometimes they're not getting a reply," he told the BBC.
The prime minister added that publishing salaries in adverts was also important for closing the gender pay gap.
He was also challenged over whether MPs should be disclosing salaries when advertising for staff in their offices.
A number of politicians are currently advertising for roles without giving an expected salary., external
Burnham said: "It would apply completely to them too and the call I'm making today is, before the law changes do it voluntarily because it's the right thing to do."
Greater transparency
The Cabinet Office launched a consultation into pay and reducing discrimination in the summer, and the government said there had been "overwhelming support" for greater transparency, with 94% of respondents backing the move.
"Whether you're a young person starting out or a parent trying to support your family, you should know what a job pays before spending your time and effort applying for it," Burnham said.
The government said the move was part of attempts to reduce the nearly one million young people not in education, employment or training - or "Neet" - ahead of the final report of the Milburn Review into youth inactivity, which is due in the coming weeks.
Publishing salary details upfront could "expose unjustified differences in pay, give workers greater confidence to challenge discrimination and prevent disagreements over pay escalating into disputes".
The proposals are similar to measures being introduced in the European Union., external
Employers in Europe will have to disclose the initial pay or range for new roles, which must either be included in a published job advert or shared before an interview.
According to data from UK jobs website Adzuna, external, 51% of the adverts on its site in September had salary information, but the proportion has been falling in recent years.
Adzuna co-founder Andrew Hunter said being open about pay "should be the norm, not the exception".
He added that employers who put a salary on a job advert "attract more applicants, and better-suited ones".
'More complicated'
Previous research from the CIPD, external, an industry body for human resources managers, has indicated that the public sector and charities are more likely to reveal pay information that private firms, while pay ranges were more common than specific salaries.
But it found not all employers were "fully transparent", with pay ranges sometimes wider than Â£10,000.
CIPD chief executive Neil Carberry said that while, in principle, giving salary details was "a good thing", in practice it was "more complicated".
"There isn't always a single fixed figure, and employers will want to set pay based on a candidate's skills, experience and potential."
Carberry added the process was complex, saying that drafting job adverts is "best left to good employer practice rather than government regulation".
The government has said it will set out further details on what information will be required and how the legislation will be enforced "in due course".
Conservative shadow business secretary Julia Lopez said: "At a time when employers are finding it harder and harder to take on staff, Labour have decided to make their lives even more difficult.
"It should be up to businesses to decide what information they advertise about job openings, and to decide how to attract the best applicants.
"As long as they are not being dishonest, misleading or discriminatory, it should not be a matter for the government."
Last week, the Equality and Human Rights Commission (EHRC), said publishing salaries in job adverts would be a "positive step".
It also said bosses should be required to respond to questionnaires about colleagues' pay to cut pay discrimination.
At present, employers do not have to respond to employee requests for salary information about their co-workers.
The EHRC also said employers should be prevented from asking about current salary when offering a job to stop a history of discrimination from continuing.
Employers in the UK are currently allowed to ask you how much you get paid in your current role, but applicants are under no obligation to tell them.
